RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement

Delin Zhao∗ Zhengrong Yue∗ Junlin He∗ Yali Wang† Affiliation: MMLab @ SIAT
Abstract

Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent’s current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

1 Introduction

Robot agents increasingly improve their own software through interaction: RoboRSI refines reusable skills, Zetta develops critics and recovery skills, and DynaHarness revises interfaces between semantic decisions and physical execution [33, 5, 3]. Together with RAX, which turns exploration feedback into reusable programs, these systems make execution procedures revisable [11]. An equally important choice is what the agent practices next, because a fixed source leaves unprobed weaknesses outside the feedback driving revision. Improving execution alone leaves this choice unchanged.

Useful practice changes as an agent’s capabilities develop. A drawer skill that succeeds alone can still fail when composed with object placement, so practice must probe the composition as well as its individual steps. Selecting such practice requires interpreting prior outcomes, identifying prerequisites, and retaining conditions that reveal regressions. Automatic curricula already connect practice selection with skill accumulation [28], but the selection procedure itself must also adapt as failures are resolved and new interactions emerge. Earlier rules for finding informative challenges can then become inadequate. This motivates a robot self-improvement loop that revises how it chooses practice alongside how it executes tasks.

We introduce RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), in which a curriculum harness and an execution harness evolve through an adversarial interaction (Figure 1). A harness contains the prompts, skills, tools, interfaces, and agent-readable memory that organize behavior around frozen foundation models. The curriculum side uses prior capability evidence to expose weaknesses in the current execution harness. The execution side responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities, and its changing capabilities redirect the curriculum’s search. Independent agents make runtime decisions on each side, while external optimizers use the resulting evidence to install revisions for future runs.

Adversarial challenge generation requires a stable reference for judging progress, so RoboACE alternates the two updates. With execution fixed, the curriculum side revises its procedures and proposes practice; admission checks validity and consistency before fixing a comparison snapshot. The execution side then evaluates candidate revisions on that snapshot, and consolidated outcomes inform the next curriculum update. This order separates challenge selection from the response it elicits, while an infrequently invoked Strategic Advisor reviews longer histories to reconsider repetitive or stalled revision directions.

RoboACE brings together software self-improvement and evolving curricula through persistent revisions to both harnesses. RPG constructs practice from offline data and refines execution on the resulting fixed task set [32]; our curriculum side also revises the procedures that select and construct subsequent practice. POET evolves environments together with their solutions [30, 31]; our implementation instead adapts the software that organizes challenge production and robot execution around frozen models. The changing task library is an output of curriculum-harness evolution, alongside the execution revisions it prompts.

We instantiate this loop in simulated manipulation, beginning with a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions and evaluating frozen deployments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X. The final deployment outperforms the evaluated systems on all four panels (Table 2). On LIBERO-PRO, it improves over the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and over direct execution by the same VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies show how evidence-reading guidance changes independent practice selection and how execution revisions clarify skill grounding and controller handoffs. Together, the framework and empirical study establish a concrete implementation of robot self-improvement in which both the practice-selection procedure and the execution software remain open to revision.

2 Related Work

Embodied agents around foundation models.

Agent software connects foundation-model reasoning to physical control. Code as Policies expresses closed-loop robot behavior as language-model programs [16], while CaP-X evaluates robot coding agents and the use of execution feedback for skill synthesis [9]. RPent augments a controller with prompt-based experience [34], and VoLo combines subgoal decomposition, VLM monitoring, and grasp replanning around a VLA controller [2]. Related systems also organize closed-loop control through execution-aware agent harnesses [6, 18]. Our focus is the revision of such harnesses across rounds, together with the procedures that determine which challenges those rounds contain.

Embodied self-improvement.

Execution feedback can support persistent changes to robot software. RoboRSI structures reusable skill improvement and provides the execution infrastructure used in our implementation [33]. Zetta develops runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen policy [5], and DynaHarness uses contracts and failure-driven revisions to connect semantic decisions with execution [3]. RAX and ASPIRE convert exploration into programs and skills [11, 20]; EmbodiedEvo distills physical feedback into code skills and diagnostic lessons [15]. RPG generates simulated practice from offline data before refining prompts and skills on that task set [32], while EmbodiedRSI selects experiments to distinguish hypotheses about code and skill changes [27]. RoboACE extends the object of revision to the curriculum harness that uses execution evidence to select and construct future practice.

Curriculum and challenge evolution.

Changing challenges can guide learning toward abilities that a fixed task source overlooks. Voyager connects automatic curricula with skill accumulation [28], and Eureka generates reward functions for robot training [21]. POET jointly develops environments and solutions [30, 31], PAIRED uses regret to guide environment design [4], and asymmetric self-play builds robotic curricula through proposer and solver roles [23]. Eurekaverse generates environment programs [17]; OMNI-EPIC produces tasks and rewards in response to learning progress [7]; GenEnv co-evolves agent and environment policies [10]. In RoboACE, both the challenge-selection procedures and the execution procedures receive persistent software revisions while foundation-model weights remain fixed.

Pretrained robot control.

Generalist controllers supply action priors learned from large robot datasets. OpenVLA and π0.5\pi_{0.5} illustrate this approach [13, 1], while OpenVLA-OFT improves the fine-tuning and inference recipe and π0\pi_{0}-FAST studies efficient action tokenization [12, 24]. Harness adaptation changes how an agent invokes such controllers, combines them with other tools, and responds to feedback. We use π0.5\pi_{0.5} as the frozen controller throughout development and revise the software around it.

3 Adversarial Co-Evolution of Robot Harnesses

3.1 Framework Overview

RoboACE takes prior capability evidence and the current pair of harnesses as input and returns revised harnesses together with evidence for the next round. The curriculum harness guides practice selection and construction; the execution harness organizes planning, code skills, and pretrained control. Each contains reusable prompts, skills, tools, interfaces, and agent-readable memory. All foundation-model weights remain frozen. Figure 2 shows how the two sides exchange evidence while updating in alternating phases.

Each side separates runtime decisions from persistent revision. An independent agent runs its harness to propose practice or attempt a task. An external optimizer examines the resulting evidence, proposes changes, and tests them through further independent runs. We call the accepted harness version Stable and a proposed revision Candidate. A phase can retain its incoming Stable version, and its revision history records the tests and the reasons for adoption or rejection. The Strategic Advisor can review evidence across multiple local updates without taking over these decisions.

In round kk, the curriculum side receives the prior Capability Profile PkP_{k} and a fixed execution deployment. Its admitted proposals and the internal benchmark form a fixed task snapshot 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k}. The execution side first measures its incoming deployment on this snapshot, then tests revisions and selects a deployment. Consolidated execution evidence yields Pk+1P_{k+1}. This ordering separates the curriculum’s prediction of useful practice from the difficulty and response measured afterward. Appendix A specifies the operational protocol.

3.2 Phase 1: Evolving the Curriculum Harness

The curriculum must choose conditions that reveal actionable gaps in the current execution capability. Its agent reads PkP_{k}, which summarizes demonstrated abilities, applicable lessons, unresolved gaps, and uncertainty. Using this profile, task statistics, and descriptions of available tasks or assets, the agent retains, replaces, or adds practice conditions. Selection balances new challenges with prerequisites and familiar conditions that can expose regressions; increasing difficulty alone is not the objective.

The curriculum optimizer revises how the agent makes these choices. It tests whether a candidate harness supports better use of evidence, maintains coverage, and recovers from failed retrieval or construction. The revised assets persist across future curriculum-agent runs, whose practice choices remain independent. Section 4.4 illustrates this distinction through a revision to evidence-reading guidance and the retrieval interface.

Admission and handoff.

A challenge must qualify before it replaces an existing condition. Native tasks retain their source definitions and initializations. For constructed worlds, admission checks physical validity and reachability, then a Judge checks agreement among the instruction, goal, and scene. Failed or inconclusive checks return the proposal for revision. These checks use no fresh VLA rollouts to pre-screen difficulty and do not certify a complete executable solution. A separate Benchmark Curator maintains reference coverage and core anchors. At handoff, the curriculum deployment is fixed, and admitted practice and internal benchmark conditions form 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k}. Task definitions and initializations remain fixed throughout the execution phase. Appendix A.2 details the checks.

3.3 Phase 2: Evolving the Execution Harness

The execution phase turns the admitted challenges into evidence for reusable changes. The execution agent first attempts 𝒯k\mathcal{T}_{k} with the incoming Stable harness. It chooses among code skills and VLA control, which can address a whole task or a shorter language goal. The environment’s native predicate determines task completion, so a successful local operation, such as grasping an object, can still leave the overall task unfinished.

The execution optimizer diagnoses failures from outcomes, trajectories, public observations, and tool feedback. Diagnosis distinguishes failures of a skill from misleading skill descriptions or inappropriate tool choices, because these require different revisions. Candidate changes are tested through independent agent runs with task definitions, initializations, model settings, and budgets held fixed. Conditions shared by practice and the internal benchmark use the same execution record. Targeted runs diagnose individual mechanisms, while comparisons across the full snapshot inform adoption. The optimizer considers successes, regressions, reuse, and cost before installing Candidate or retaining Stable.

3.4 Closing the Loop with Execution Evidence

Execution outcomes must inform future practice without exposing evidence reserved for other roles. The Experience Consolidator converts permitted task-level results and lessons into Pk+1P_{k+1}. The curriculum receives this profile and task statistics, through which unresolved gaps can prompt new challenges and resolved gaps can redirect practice. Raw images, trajectories, model and tool calls, and implementation differences remain on the execution side. Geometry reserved for the Judge remains outside the execution agent’s observations.

A diagnosis becomes useful to future agents only when it reaches a deployable prompt, skill description, or retrievable manual. The optimizer checks whether the agent actually receives and uses the revised material. Persistent assets are versioned with each deployment and kept separate from episode workspaces. Appendix A.3 describes this interface. Final evaluation remains outside the loop and does not inform curriculum choices or version selection.

3.5 Long-Horizon Strategic Guidance

Local revisions can repeatedly address nearby failures while leaving the broader direction of improvement unexamined. The Strategic Advisor offers an infrequent, on-demand review across multiple updates. It reads the requesting optimizer’s permitted evidence and revision history to identify recurring failures, stalled revision patterns, and gaps in coverage. Its output proposes directions for investigation rather than installing harness changes.

The local optimizer translates this advice into experiments, evaluates the evidence, and decides which revisions to adopt. Recommendations about the inactive side wait for that side’s next update phase. This separation allows a longer view of the campaign while preserving the alternating comparison protocol and local responsibility for adoption.

4 Empirical Study

We evaluate whether the final frozen deployment improves over its initial version and alternative controllers or agent systems. We then examine recorded revisions to identify how the curriculum and execution harnesses changed during development.

4.1 Development and Evaluation Scope

We instantiated RoboACE with GPT-6.1 (Terra) and pretrained tools including SAM 3 and π0.5\pi_{0.5} control [1]. The campaign maintained 30 practice conditions and an internal benchmark of up to 40 conditions, with 27 saved round records. Both harnesses received persistent software revisions; no LLM or VLA weights were trained or fine-tuned by this project.

Development remained within the LIBERO ecosystem. The evolving practice libraries included 76 distinct native LIBERO conditions across rounds, together with constructed worlds that passed admission. Evaluation tests transfer both to reserved LIBERO conditions and to LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X. Development uses only LIBERO conditions. The held-out LIBERO panel is condition-disjoint from the audited development history, while LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, and LIBERO-X are not used during development.

We used four fixed panels of 200 conditions each [19, 8, 35, 29] (Table 1). LIBERO contains 40 tasks with five reserved initializations per task. LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-PRO use fixed perturbation subsets, while LIBERO-X includes 40 conditions at each challenge level, including language-paired conditions. These panels define the evaluation in this study and do not constitute the complete official benchmark protocols.

4.2 Compared Systems and Measurement

The core comparison includes RoboACE (before evolution), RoboACE (after evolution), and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [1]. The π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline uses the final system’s official VLA controller continuously, without an upper-level LLM or other skills. Initial and final agents use Terra/high at evaluation. The controller baseline shares the final agent’s controller, while the systems differ in orchestration and available tools. We also evaluate released OpenVLA-OFT [12], π0\pi_{0}-FAST [24], Cosmos Policy [14], and GR00T N1.7 [22] without an upper-level LLM.

The agent comparisons use RPent without target-benchmark experience [34] and VoLo [2]. RPent receives a neutral prompt without target-experience retrieval. VoLo combines subgoal decomposition, VLM monitoring, and grasp replanning. Both use Terra/high, official π0.5\pi_{0.5} control, and public observations without hidden geometric state. Appendix A.4 specifies the baseline variants, controller interfaces, and serving configurations.

Table 2 includes model-author reports [25, 26] and published benchmark results [8].

Our evaluation runs use the environment’s native task predicate. All systems in our evaluation share a per-episode budget of 8,000 environment control steps at 20 Hz (6 min 40 s of simulation time). π0.5\pi_{0.5} executes continuous five-action chunks.

For our evaluations, each cell contains one designated observation for every assigned condition. Historical prefix observations are retained without choosing the best of repeated attempts. Success rate is the number of confirmed native successes divided by all 200 conditions; timeouts, infrastructure errors, and all other outcomes count as failures. Only complete, independently audited panels are scored. The results characterize one development trajectory and its resulting deployments.

4.3 System-Level Performance

The final RoboACE deployment outperforms all evaluated systems on the four fixed panels (Table 2). Relative to the initial deployment, it improves by 35.5 percentage points on LIBERO and by 30.0 points on LIBERO-Plus. The gain is 15.0 points on LIBERO-PRO and 11.0 points on LIBERO-X. These comparisons measure the overall change between the initial and final deployments, including their accumulated harness revisions.

π0.5\pi_{0.5} is close to the final deployment on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, while the separation grows on LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-X (Figure 3). On LIBERO-PRO, RoboACE exceeds π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 13.5 percentage points; on LIBERO-X, the margin is 19.0 points. Sharing the official controller makes this comparison informative about the complete agent system built around pretrained control. RoboACE also exceeds the strongest evaluated agent baseline on every panel. Its margins are 1.5 and 4.5 percentage points on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, respectively, and 13.5 and 18.0 points on LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-X.

4.4 Case Studies of Harness Evolution

Curriculum revision changes how evidence is used.

An optional compact evidence reader initially went unused. A revision to prompts and the retrieval interface explained selective reading, coverage checks, and targeted recovery after truncation (Figure 4(a)). In a subsequent independent run, the curriculum agent used the reader and produced a valid 30-condition course with two replacements of its own choosing. The persistent revision concerned the procedure for using evidence, while the agent retained responsibility for selecting the practice conditions.

Execution revision clarifies a skill’s grounding contract.

Earlier evidence indicated that standalone drawer skills did not reliably compose. Before receiving fresh execution outcomes, the curriculum agent retained 27 conditions and added top-drawer closure, pudding placement followed by closure, and bottom-drawer opening. The ensuing execution revision clarified the difference between a front-panel localization seed and the attached handle (Figure 4(b)). Skill descriptions now required resolving that handle and verifying the target drawer before motion. Successes across the full 54-condition comparison snapshot changed from 48 to 50. The record connects a curriculum-selected composition challenge to a persistent clarification of the execution interface.

Strategic review connects failures across local revisions.

Repeated recovery remained a shared bottleneck after changes to grasping, drawer recovery, and motion interfaces. The Strategic Advisor reviewed this history and identified a broader question: when should the agent continue VLA control, switch to a code skill, or intervene in an ongoing attempt (Figure 5)? Whole-task VLA capability does not ensure reliable behavior under arbitrary language subgoals. The resulting guidance preserved task intent, targeted specific controller limitations, and required checking prerequisites before a handoff. The record illustrates how longer-horizon review can connect recurring local failures to a common question about control selection.

5 Conclusion

We presented RoboACE, a robot self-improvement framework that revises both the selection of practice and the software used to execute it. A curriculum harness proposes challenges from prior capability evidence, and an execution harness responds with persistent revisions around frozen foundation models. Alternating phases connect the two through admitted tasks, fixed comparison snapshots, and consolidated feedback.

The final deployment achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated systems on four LIBERO-family panels, with gains of up to 35.5 percentage points over the initial deployment. Recorded cases show changes to practice selection, skill grounding, and controller intervention. These results support adversarial harness co-evolution as a concrete approach to joint curriculum and execution revision. Establishing its behavior across independent campaigns, broader environments, and physical robots is the next empirical step.

Appendix A Implementation and Evaluation Details

This appendix specifies the update boundaries, task admission, deployable memory, and baseline evaluation underlying Sections 3 and 4.

A.1 Operational Update Protocol

The curriculum proposes new conditions using prior capability evidence; fresh execution observations arrive only after handoff. The curriculum phase uses only the prior-round capability profile; execution outcomes on newly admitted conditions are collected after the task snapshot is fixed. Candidate execution comparisons preserve task definitions and initializations. These boundaries distinguish practice selection, incoming difficulty, candidate behavior, and the evidence used for adoption (Table 3).

A.2 Task Validation and Admission

Native tasks preserve their source definitions and initialization identities. Constructed tasks additionally pass compilation and physical-validity checks for loadability, stable finite states, valid goal references, and absence of severe interpenetration. Geometry checks use the compiled robot and inverse kinematics to assess the reachability of key interaction endpoints. The Judge then reviews semantic agreement among the instruction, goal, and actual scene.

Failed or inconclusive proposals return to the curriculum agent for revision. Constructed tasks are admitted after checks for compilation, physical validity, endpoint reachability, and instruction-goal-scene consistency. These checks do not guarantee full dynamic executability, and task difficulty is not pre-screened with fresh VLA rollouts. Recorded selections include both native tasks and admitted constructed worlds.

A.3 Deployable Memory Interface

The implementation exposes up to 2500 characters from each skill’s main description and supports retrieval of additional task and skill manuals. The optimizer checks whether the agent receives and uses the relevant material. An optimizer journal can contain a useful diagnosis without making it accessible to future agents; deployment requires incorporating it into an exposed description, prompt, or retrievable manual. Episode workspaces remain separate from persistent assets, whose code, tool, and memory versions are fixed with the deployment.

A.4 Evaluation Identities and Controller Interfaces

Direct π0.5\pi_{0.5} continuously uses the final system’s official controller, executing five actions per prediction chunk without an upper-level LLM or other skills. Initial and final agents use Terra/high. All systems in our evaluation share a per-episode budget of 8,000 environment control steps at 20 Hz (6 min 40 s of simulation time).

Released-model baselines.

OpenVLA-OFT uses the released combined spatial/object/goal/10 fine-tuned checkpoint with native eight-action chunks, front and wrist images, and proprioception. π0\pi_{0}-FAST uses the official pi0_fast_libero checkpoint, released image, state, and action transforms, and five-action replanning from a ten-action horizon. This project neither trains nor fine-tunes these models.

Agent-baseline variants.

RPent uses a neutral prompt without target-experience retrieval, rather than its experience-augmented variant. VoLo retains its deployed adapter’s subgoal decomposition, monitoring, and replanning, including VLM monitoring and replan_grasp. Both use Terra/high, official π0.5\pi_{0.5} control, and public observations without hidden geometric state.

A.5 Complete-Panel Checks and Recording

A released-model panel requires 200 unique request/result pairs, settled workers, and an independent audit of source identity, raw records, and outcome counts. Agent-baseline panels likewise require 200 complete, independently audited conditions. Partial panels are excluded from scored results.

Each condition contributes one designated main-table observation. Historical prefix observations remain in place without best-attempt selection. Timeouts and infrastructure outcomes remain in the denominator and count as failures. Separate reassessments and targeted diagnostics do not replace the designated main-table observations.
